qt: to the Commission Per Clausen (The Left) Subject:

At a time when the focus is on both Europe’s digital sovereignty and the need for innovation, both are threatened by what many describe as Google’s de facto lockdown of the Android system for independent app developers1 (including, potentially, European public authorities). Among other things, these changes mean all developers – even those who do not distribute their programmes via Google’s tools, or who create apps for their own use – MUST register with Google and pay a fee to the company. Moreover, these changes mean that phones running on a system that was marketed as open will no longer be open; instead, Google will have ultimate control and the ability to lock down applications and decide what people are allowed to install on their own devices. In light of the above, could the European Commission answer the following questions: 1.
Google’s plans can only harm innovation and competition in the app market, so what steps will the Commission take in response?
If Google can lock down public applications, does the Commission not consider this to be a potential security risk?
at: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.11.2026) The Commission is aware of Google’s announcement to introduce a developer verification process. Article 6(4) of the Digital Markets Act (DMA)1 obliges Google to allow and technically enable the effective distribution of apps on their operating system through third party app stores or the web. It also permits Google to introduce strictly necessary and proportionate measures to ensure that third-party software apps and third-party software application stores do not endanger the integrity of Google’s hardware or operating system, provided that such measures are duly justified. Subject to the same conditions, Google is also permitted to apply measures and settings enabling end users to effectively protect security in relation to thirdparty software apps and third-party software application stores. The Commission is actively engaged in a regulatory dialogue with Google and is diligently monitoring its compliance with the DMA to ensure that apps, including public apps, can be effectively distributed on Google Android OS outside Google Play. Moreover, the EU Open Source Strategy2 leverages open source as a key instrument for strengthening the EU’s technological sovereignty by reducing dependencies on non-EU proprietary IT, fostering interoperable and secure digital ecosystems, and supporting the development of a full European technology stack. It explicitly identifies operating systems as an important area for action. In this context, a first 10 million EUR grant from Horizon Europe focusing on open-source operating systems will soon be signed and announced at the next Free and Open Source Developers' European Meeting.
